zh-HK/securityPage.json::securityPage.pu: Scope a rule to a single table, or to a whole domain so it covers every table in it; where both apply, the table rule wins for that table. A rule is written against a role rather than a person, so what someone can see is changed by changing the role they hold.

A row-level security rule is a SQL predicate bound to one role and one scope. The server ANDs it into the query before execution — on reads and on writes, whichever surface the request arrives on — so a role sees only the rows its rule permits and cannot opt out by picking a different client.
zh-HK/securityPage.json::securityPage.ro: A role also carries its own ceilings: requests per second, and limits on query depth, node count, and execution time. That is how a role can be given reach without being given unbounded cost — an expensive query is refused by the role that issued it, not by the source it would have hit.

A role is the unit every other permission is written against. Its capabilities decide which operations it may run, and its domain access decides which parts of the model it can reach at all. Row-level rules, and the access checks on every surface, name a role rather than a person — so what someone can see and do is changed by changing the role they hold.

Only matters when Provisa runs as several instances behind a load balancer. It decides whether the materialized view is ONE copy shared by all instances, or a separate copy per instance. Shared: a single copy in the shared store, refreshed by one instance at a time (a short lease with fencing), so every instance reads the same consistent snapshot — pick this when instances must agree. Per-instance: each instance builds and refreshes its own copy independently — simpler and faster, but instances can briefly disagree (eventually consistent), so only safe for a deterministic view over a source that's stable within a refresh cycle. Where the copy lives depends on the federation engine's store: per-instance only makes sense when each instance has its OWN store (e.g. an embedded/in-process DuckDB). With a SHARED external store (Postgres, Trino + object store, a warehouse) every instance writes the same physical table, so use shared — per-instance has nowhere private to write and would just clobber.

How each update is written to the MV's store. Its options depend on Time Travel (keep history): OFF stores current state only — replace (overwrite everything) or upsert (merge by primary key); ON keeps history — snapshot (append the whole fresh result as a new version each refresh) or delta (append only the rows that changed, plus tombstones for deletes). Snapshot/delta are the bitemporal storage modes, which the engine uses in place of replace/upsert.

Optional preflight check run after the view SQL and before landing: define preflight(streams, ctx) and return a VERDICT — ctx.ok() to continue, ctx.abort(reason) to reject (error + poison downstream), or ctx.quarantine(reason) to hold without landing. streams is a dict keyed by input node: streams["schema.table"] yields that input's rows lazily, so you inspect an input without materializing it. A check inspects; it does NOT transform rows (put transforms in SQL or an external processor). A SQL-expressible check — if any(...)/all(...) over one input's rows — is pushed down to the engine as a count probe over that input, so it scales to a billion rows; anything else streams each input as Arrow batches and short-circuits. Call ctx.warn(reason) for a non-fatal advisory. It MUST be deterministic — no clock, randomness, imports, or IO — and is purity-checked when you save; a non-deterministic or unsafe check is rejected.

How the freshness probe detects change, gated by source type. watermark → append (fetch rows past MAX(watermark)); hash → replace (content token, e.g. ETag/checksum); count → replace (row-count delta, coarse); none → replace on cadence (the output content-hash still suppresses an unchanged ripple). Keeps history (time travel), compactly. Every refresh appends ONLY the rows that changed (plus tombstones for deletes) as new versions — you can still query 'as of' any time, but storage grows only by the change, not the whole result. The classic way to maintain a full change history / audit trail of a source without storing a full copy each refresh. Needs an entity key to identify the entity across versions.

The query is NOT re-run. The single input delivers the rows that changed (as a delta), and only those rows are merged into the stored table by primary key — so work per refresh scales with the SIZE OF THE CHANGE, not the whole dataset. The cheapest option for large, slowly-changing data. It applies only when all three hold: (1) exactly ONE input (no joins), (2) that input emits a delta — i.e. it runs on a change/CDC signal, not full snapshots, and (3) the view SQL is a plain column projection (no join, filter, GROUP BY, aggregate, DISTINCT, or computed column) so the input's delta maps 1:1 to this view's delta. Also needs a primary key. If a refresh brings no delta (a full-snapshot input or a probe trigger), it falls back to a full recompute for that refresh.

Current state, no history. Every refresh re-runs the whole query and replaces the stored table with the fresh result. Simplest and always correct. Work per refresh scales with the TOTAL size of the inputs, not with how much actually changed.

Keeps history (time travel). Every refresh appends the ENTIRE fresh result as a new version stamped with its time — you can query the table 'as of' any past refresh. Simplest history model and works on any engine, but storage grows by the full result size every refresh.

Current state, no history. Every refresh re-runs the whole query, then merges the result into the stored table by primary key: matching rows are updated in place, new rows inserted, nothing deleted-and-reinserted. The query still recomputes everything, so work scales with total input size — only the write is by key.

🧭 This compass reopens the tour anytime. Leave whenever — click the app or press Esc.

Provisa is one model that holds your data, its metadata and the processing between them. The same model defines your data estate and operates it — it is all one thing, and it stays out of the data path.

That is why everything stays in sync, and why reuse is built in: a relationship, metric, mask or rule defined once serves every surface, environment and role. Duplicate tables and metrics, duplicate commands and rules, even two systems serving the same data sit side by side in the model, so duplication is easy to see and simple to remove.

It is compact, extensible and composable. It slots in beside what you have, brings order to the sprawl, and lets every data professional apply their expertise without limiting their imagination — it only removes the drudgery.

🎯 The core is one short exercise: connect a database, then query it in the language or tool you already use — or just ask in plain English. About five minutes, right from your desktop, with no infrastructure to stand up.

zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step15.descr:
A relationship does two jobs. It shapes your data model: how tables across sources and domains connect — which is what every query surface follows, whether GraphQL nesting, Cypher paths or SQL joins.

It is also a rule. Joins are governed: a role without the ignore_relationships right can join only along registered relationships, so which ones exist decides which queries are legal. Grant that right deliberately to a role you trust and it joins freely (never in high-security mode).

Relationships link tables across sources — even across different databases — turning flat tables into a traversable graph.

zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step20.descr:
🔧 Compose your whole delivery pipeline right here — no separate ETL tool:
  • 👁️ Views — over any table, ephemeral or materialized, and views over views.
  • ⚡ Commands — governed, typed operations (an HTTP service, a Python model, a stored procedure) that do double duty: a step inside your pipeline, and a first-class API that downstream apps and agents call to act on your data — invokable from every surface, fully governed and traced.
  • ⭐ Entities & facts — declare a dimension or fact once and Provisa generates the warehouse, methodology-neutral: 3NF (Inmon), star schema (Kimball), or Data Vault.
  • 📏 Metrics — governed aggregate definitions (“net revenue”) with grain bound at query time. Define once; every surface — SQL, GraphQL, AI agents — computes the same number, and views built on a metric regenerate when its definition changes.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step20.title: Build your delivery pipeline
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step21.descr:
🏗️ Materialize a view and you get a full ETL engine, declared not scripted:
  • 📅 Scheduled snapshots on real business calendars — recurrence rules, holidays, business-day gating, and a close grace period, so it fires on your reporting calendar, not just a clock.
  • 🗄️ Store As… — replace, upsert, or keep history with snapshot / delta, plus incremental compute.
  • 🕰️ Time travel — bitemporal history; query the model as of any point in time.
  • ⚡ Near-real-time refresh with debounce, or freshness-driven republish as inputs change.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step21.title: Materialize into a live warehouse
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step22.descr:
🧬 Lineage is the dependency trail your derivations leave: what each view, calculated column or metric is built from, and what depends on it. This is a real query, analyzed — follow name_upper back through its transforms to the exact source columns that feed it.

Nothing runs — the query is only analyzed.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step22.title: Lineage, end to end
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step23.descr:
The Admin pages run the platform:
  • ⚙️ Choose and configure your federation engine — pluggable: DuckDB (embedded, zero-config), Trino, PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, or a cloud warehouse as a first-class engine (Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks, Microsoft Fabric, Azure Synapse). Swap it anytime — the model, the surfaces, and the governance above it never change.
  • 🔗 Whichever engine you pick brings its own live external data reach — Parquet, Iceberg, Delta read in place, zero-copy, credentials auto-provisioned. Anything it can't link live lands as a governed replica.
  • 🔑 Manage encryption keys and wire up auth providers
  • 📊 Full observability — redirect to any OpenTelemetry collector for enterprise-class trace management
  • 📤 Export the model's configuration — the whole model or chosen sections — as a file to review, diff and ship through CI/CD

The same model travels from local dev to production, validated at every step — no rewrite:

  • Develop — embedded DuckDB, no Docker. Build & validate locally.
  • Validate at scale — Docker, spin up an engine + observability. Prove behavior against production engines.
  • Promote — point at your own infrastructure, build through CI/CD, ship to production.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step23.title: Operate it

Whatever the source — a Mongo collection, a Kafka topic, a REST endpoint, a graph — Provisa decomposes it into a 2D table: one uniform shape to query across every source.

📁 Group tables into domains, each owned by a data steward who guards the model's quality as it evolves.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step4.title: Everything becomes a table
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step5.descri:
Choose a source, schema, and table, then pick columns — each with its own policy:
  • 🎭 Masking — redact values per role
  • 👁️ Visibility — show or hide the column
  • 🏷️ Aliases — rename for the model

That's the whole setup — a source and a few tables. 🚀 Now let's query it. →
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step5.title: Pick columns & policy
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step6.descri:
SQL lives in the SQL explorer. Standard SQL federated across every source — join Postgres to Mongo to a CSV in one statement. And the model's own metadata and every activity trace are themselves queryable tables here — join your audit log or lineage straight to live data.

🔌 Not just this explorer — the same governed SQL runs through multiple wire protocols; your tool picks the one it already speaks:

  • pgwire — every Postgres-compatible client — psql, DBeaver, Tableau, Power BI — connects out of the box.
  • JDBC — drops into any Java/JVM app, ETL pipeline, or JDBC-capable BI tool.
  • Arrow Flight SQL — columnar streaming for ADBC clients — no row re-encoding, built for large result sets.
  • DuckDB · airport — ATTACH Provisa from DuckDB and query the governed federation in place.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step6.title: SQL (1 of 7 surfaces)
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step7.descri:
◈ The same query, typed as GraphQL:

{ inquiries { groupBy { user }, count } }

Grouping and aggregates over your relationships — 🎯 one endpoint, 📖 self-documenting schema.

🔌 Hit it from any GraphQL client — Apollo, Relay, urql — and, with federation enabled, drop Provisa into an Apollo supergraph as a subgraph, so your federated model composes alongside your existing graphs.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step7.title: GraphQL (2 of 7 surfaces)
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step8.descri:
🕸️ Traverse the federated model as a graph with Cypher:

MATCH (u:Users)-[:SUBMITTED]->(i:Inquiries)

↔️ That traversal runs across sources — no single graph database required.

🔌 And any Bolt client — Neo4j Browser, Bloom — runs that same traversal over the wire, no code change.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step8.title: Cypher (3 of 7 surfaces)
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step9.descri:
⚙️ Every registered entity is also a gRPC service:

rpc QueryInquiries(...) returns (...)

Call it from any gRPC client — 📐 strongly typed, 🚀 high-throughput.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.step9.title: gRPC (4 of 7 surfaces)
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepDataProd:
📦 Every product here speaks ODPS (the Open Data Product Standard) — owner, team, purpose, limitations, usage, SLA, support, custom properties — and Provisa auto-publishes it straight into Snowflake Horizon and BigQuery Dataplex, so it shows up as a native product in the catalog your consumers already use.

🔁 There's no separate export step to forget: the spec is derived from the live model — tables, lineage, tags, glossary terms — every time, so what's published can't drift out of date the way a hand-maintained ODPS file would.

✅ Each product also carries the glossary terms that define its columns and the data-quality results of the checkers that scan it.
Data products, published where consumers already look
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepEnvKinds: A non-production environment is read or read-write. A read-write environment keeps its own changes, and a write never reaches a source. Turn on Test data and every column shows its fake, with unfaked personal data shown as NULL.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepFakes.de: 🎭 The column list's Test data mode shows each column's fake, such as email(). Fake only the identifying columns and keep the rest real. A column can also carry a synthetic rule, used only when generating synthetic data.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepFakesFil: ✨ Fill from profile proposes fakes for identifying columns, and synthetic rules for the rest, from the table's latest profile. Nothing saves until you save the form.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepGlossary: 📖 Every term links back to the columns that carry it — curate names, definitions, and typed relationships (kind-of, part-of, synonym-of) by hand, or let AI fill in the gaps: ✨ Definitions drafts only the terms still missing one, and ✨ Relationships proposes links across the whole glossary. Flag a term excluded from export to keep it out of published metadata.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepPolly.de:
💬 Polly sets Provisa up in plain language — much easier than reading the docs.

“register my Postgres” · “fake the email column in the customers table” · “create a QA environment on synthetic data” · “who can see salaries?”

Polly works through the same governed APIs and rights as the UI, so it can only do what you can. Polly is open here; the chat button reopens this panel anytime.
👀 Expand a row and click Preview — live data through the governed pipeline: masked, access-controlled, and server-paged, so even a billion-row table opens instantly. Filters, sorts, and grouping run inside the query, and API-backed tables prompt for their required parameters first.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepProfiler: Every run is compared with the table's recent runs, and a measure that drifts is flagged. A data-quality checker raises the exception. You can also accept constraints the profile proposes, and check runs against expectations from outside Provisa. A constraint can also be exported as a check in the contract of a Soda or Great Expectations checker.
Pick a profiler and save, then use Run Profile Now and View Profile Runs. Results land as tables you register and govern like any other. Until you register them, no reader sees a profile.
📊 Edit any table to add it to a Data Profiler, a source that profiles its member tables on a schedule: column shapes, distributions, value frequencies and children per parent.
📤 Publish it where your org already looks. Catalog entries (tables, columns, domains, stewards, approved relationships), data products and column-level lineage go out, and each target receives what it supports: DataHub, OpenMetadata, Collibra, Atlan and Apache Atlas as catalogs, Snowflake Horizon and BigQuery Dataplex as data-product listings, and lineage over OpenLineage.

Publication is outbound only: Provisa never reads a target back as a source of truth.
Publish to the tools your org uses
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityP: ✅ Write the contract by hand or build checks column by column — null rates, row counts, ranges, freshness — and dry-run it before saving. Every scan appends, so this table is the quality history: chart it, alert on it, join it to anything.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQualityT: 🧪 A data-quality checker — Soda or Great Expectations — registers as a source. It scans back through Provisa's own postgres endpoint, so one contract dialect covers a Snowflake table, an Iceberg table and a Mongo collection alike. Its results land as an ordinary table: expand the row and open it like any other.
A quality checker is just a source
📊 The audit log you queried earlier also feeds ready-made reports — usage ranking, PII access, policy denials, query health — each a governed view in the ops domain. Adding your own takes one SQL statement, and it becomes a cataloged, exportable data product like any other table.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepSyntheti: 🧪 A synthetic dataset fills a non-production environment with rows shaped like your profiled tables, with the same relationships and fan-out, at any scale. A comparison report shows how close it came.
🔒 Declare a dataset private with a privacy budget ε. Calibrated noise is added to every statistic the generator draws from a profile, and the report states what the noise dropped.

zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepQuery.de: 💬 You ask in the language or tool you already use — SQL, GraphQL, Cypher, plain language through Polly, or a BI tool or driver — and every one reads the same governed model, so the answer and the rules are the same whichever you pick.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRelsSugg: ✨ The sparkle button looks for likely joins: it reads the foreign keys your sources declare and, when an AI model key is configured, asks the model to infer more. Nothing is declared until you accept a candidate, and a rejected one stays out until you clear the rejections.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRelsList: 📋 The model's relationships, whether or not a source declares them, filterable and sortable. Expand a row to edit it or add its reverse. A role joins only along these relationships unless it holds the ignore_relationships right.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRoleInhe: 👪 A role can inherit from a parent: it receives the parent's grants, column visibility and row rules, and its own row rule for a table replaces the parent's. The role also carries its capabilities and its rate and complexity limits.
🗂️ A domain groups tables, and its data steward governs that part of the model: who sees what, masks and row rules, sensitive data, and its glossary and data products.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepTags.des: 🏷️ A tag is one org-wide label with a fixed meaning, applied to sources, tables, columns, relationships or commands. Tags carry behavior, not only documentation, and a tag can require a reason, an expiry date or a parameter when it is applied.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRequests: ✋ This request comes from someone who may not create relationships themselves, often from outside your domain, wanting to relate their tables to yours — usually the first step toward asking for your data. Relationships are governed, so approving one changes which queries are legal: a role that may join only along approved relationships can now join across it. A relationship request needs two approvals before it can be executed. A relationship across two domains needs a yes from each side. Approve it, execute it, or reject it with a reason from a fixed list; resolved requests move to the Resolved tab.
📏 A metric is the business definition of a measure, an aggregate over one fact table. Define it once and SQL, GraphQL, the explore canvas and every view built from it compute the same number; a view regenerates when its metric changes.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepCommands: ⚡ A command is a governed, typed operation, such as an HTTP service, a Python model or a stored procedure. Register it once and call it from every surface, with the same rights and tracing as a query.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepProductF: 📦 Name the owner and team, the purpose, usage, SLA and support, then pick the tables and commands it contains. These are the fields that get published. A table joins a product only when both share the same domain.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepGlossary: 📖 A term names one business concept, lists the columns that carry it and says what it means. Terms for real columns are derived for you; add one by hand for a concept no single column carries.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepObservab: 🔭 Tracing records one span per request. The Debug tracing tab adds a span per pipeline stage and per source call, with SQL text. It adds load, so turn it on for one org, role or source for a set time; it turns itself off when the time is up.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepCache.de: 🗄️ These layers are separate. The response cache holds query results, and a request opts in with @cached or a SQL comment. Small lookup tables are mirrored to speed joins. A replica of a source table that cannot be attached lives in the durable store, beside materialized views.
zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepSchedule: ⏱️ Run a webhook or a SQL statement on a cron schedule. A SQL task runs as a role you choose, so governance applies, and each task shows its last and next run.

zh-HK/tour.json::tour.steps.stepRelsAgen:
🤖 The model and its relationships are available to AI agents — Polly, and agents connecting over MCP — and they shape the queries those agents write.

An agent runs under a role, so the same rule applies to it as to a person: a query that joins outside the registered relationships fails. This is enforced, not advisory.

It is also your choice. To let an agent discover relationships, grant its role the ignore_relationships right; to keep it inside guardrails, leave the role without it. It is the same deliberate grant as for a trusted identity (never honored in high-security mode).
